intro: Hey everyone — I'm Dr. Sarah Reyes. I study how fast your brain can react to what your senses pick up. Every time you catch a falling cup or hit the brakes, your brain runs a race: sense the event, decide what to do, send the signal to your muscles. Today we're going to measure that race — first with your eyes, then with your ears — and compare the two. You'll leave with a real data set that tells you something about your own nervous system.
act1Predict: A typical visual reaction time is about 250 milliseconds — a quarter of a second. That's the time it takes for light to hit your retina, travel up the optic nerve, reach your visual cortex, get processed, trigger a decision in your motor cortex, and travel down your spinal cord to your finger. Before we measure yours, take a guess: how fast do you think you are?
act2Visual: Round 1 — eyes. Watch the panel. When it flashes green, hit the spacebar as fast as you can. Don't try to anticipate the flash — the delay is random, and pressing too early counts as a false start. Ten trials gives us a small but useful distribution. I'll be right here.
act2Audio: Round 2 — ears. Same game, different sense. When you hear the beep, hit the spacebar. Look away from the screen if it helps. Sound takes a more direct path to your brain than light — about 8 milliseconds just to reach the brainstem. Most people are faster on this round. Let's see if you are.
act3Top: Here's what we've got: two distributions, ten trials each. The median tells you your typical reaction time; the spread tells you how consistent you are. Compare your visual and audio medians. If your audio is faster, that's the direct neural pathway at work. If they're close, or your visual is faster — that's interesting too, and it's still data. The published research says visual averages around 270 ms and audio around 160 ms. How do you compare?
act3Result377: Your visual median was 377 milli seconds. Your audio median was 243 milli seconds. That's 134 milli seconds faster with your ears than your eyes — sound takes a shorter path. You guessed 333 milli seconds. Pretty close.
act3Closing: So here's what you just did: you measured a biological phenomenon — the speed of your own nervous system — using nothing but a keyboard and a screen. You generated a data set, computed summary stats, compared two distributions, and benchmarked yourself against published research. That's not just a classroom exercise. That's the scientific method, applied to you. Every trial you ran, every median you computed, is a real measurement of how your brain works.
